1. Each \(T\)-shaped polyomino covers \(4\) unit squares. Since a \(6\times 6\) grid has \(36\) squares, an area bound gives at most
   \[
   \left\lfloor \frac{36}{4}\right\rfloor=9.
   \]

2. We show \(9\) is impossible. Color the \(6\times 6\) grid like a checkerboard. It has \(18\) black and \(18\) white squares. Every \(T\)-tetromino covers either \(3\) black and \(1\) white square, or \(1\) black and \(3\) white squares.

   If \(9\) tetrominoes covered the whole board, let \(x\) be the number covering \(3\) black squares. Then the other \(9-x\) cover \(1\) black square, so the total number of black squares covered is
   \[
   3x+(9-x)=9+2x.
   \]
   This must equal \(18\), giving \(x=4.5\), impossible. Hence \(9\) pieces cannot fit, so at most \(8\) pieces can fit.

3. Eight pieces are achievable. In the diagram below, equal letters form one \(T\)-shaped polyomino, and dots are empty squares:
   \[
   \begin{array}{cccccc}
   A&A&A&B&\cdot&E\\
   C&A&B&B&E&E\\
   C&C&D&B&F&E\\
   C&D&D&D&F&F\\
   G&G&G&H&F&\cdot\\
   \cdot&G&H&H&H&\cdot
   \end{array}
   \]
   The eight letters \(A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H\) each form a \(T\)-tetromino, with \(4\) empty squares remaining.

Therefore the maximum possible number is
\[
\boxed{8}.
